drafts.title: Two readers asked for one more test, so I ran it
drafts.subtitle: One message at the empty lookup against the text null, with the same 4B model in both arms. What the test decided, and what it cannot say.
drafts.body_markdown:
After my first post, two readers asked for one more test. On dev.to, "Agentic Affairs" asked for a version in which the code retries the empty lookup. On Hashnode, "Halfcycle" suggested an error text that names the next step, and asked: "Did you try varying the error wording?" I had not.

I ran the nearest variant I could defend, the message. I did not run the retry in code. If the code repeats the lookup, the model gets the order without doing anything, so the result would say little about the model. A scripted test with no model in the repository shows how such a retry behaves.

## The set-up

- The same model in both arms, qwen3.5 4B.
- The 8 stock-note tasks under the injected empty result, chosen from run 2's failures.
- Both arms had "Retry an empty lookup once." in the system prompt.
- One arm got the empty lookup as the text `null`, as in run 2. The other got: "lookup_order returned an empty result. Call lookup_order again with the same order_id."

The test compares two arms, a baseline and a candidate. It says BLOCK when the candidate passes less often by more than 10 points. It has no verdict for "better". So I put the arm with the message in the baseline seat and run 2's set-up in the candidate seat. Here, BLOCK favours the message.

The rule and the message were pre-registered: pushed in a public commit before the first trial. This time I wrote no prediction first. A small smoke run came before the registration; its trials are not counted.

## The result

BLOCK at round 2, the earliest round at which this rule can give that verdict.

- With the message: 15 of 16 passed.
- With `null`: 2 of 16 passed.
- Pairs: 13 where only the message arm passed, 2 where both passed, 1 where both failed, 0 where only the `null` arm passed.

On these 8 tasks under the empty result, with this 4B model, this prompt and this one wording, the registered test decided that the arm with the message passes more often, by more than 10 percentage points. That holds under the test's stated assumptions, which the tool does not check. It is a threshold decision, not a measured size. The run stopped early, so 15 and 2 are counts, not rates.

## What it does not show

- Whether naming the next step is what helped. I compared one message with `null`. No message without a next step was tested.
- Anything about the 12B model.
- Anything about the other 16 tasks, the other three conditions or the full suite.
- An effect from setting these counts against run 2's: other seeds, another release.

## Two mistakes in my registration, both published

- It says nothing was changed after the smoke run. The start script gained its start checks after it.
- It says 32 of run 2's 34 failures under the empty result were on these tasks. The store gives 33 of 34.

Neither changes the tasks, the rule or the verdict.

## Check it yourself

The harness is my own open-source tool, ARCI.

- [Run 3 write-up, with the errata](https://github.com/ajaysurya1221/agent-reliability-ci/blob/main/docs/results/order-desk-study.md#run-3-2026-11-16-a-message-at-the-empty-lookup-one-model-in-both-arms)
- [The pre-registration commit](https://github.com/ajaysurya1221/agent-reliability-ci/commit/c217ae6)
- [The raw records of every trial](https://github.com/ajaysurya1221/agent-reliability-ci/tree/main/docs/results/order-desk-study)
- [The first post](https://realornoise.hashnode.dev/i-tested-whether-a-4b-model-could-replace-a-12b-one-in-a-tool-using-agent-my-first-test-was-wrong)
- [Repository](https://github.com/ajaysurya1221/agent-reliability-ci)

If you have tried it: does a message that names no next step do as well?

drafts.title: I replaced one null with one sentence at my 4B agent's empty lookup
drafts.subtitle: A third pre-registered run, asked for by two readers: what the test decided on 8 tasks, and what it does not show.
drafts.body_markdown:
In my last post, a 4B model in a small order-desk agent often stopped after an order lookup came back empty. This is what the model receives there:

```
null
```

"Agentic Affairs" on dev.to asked for a retry of the empty lookup in code. "Halfcycle" on Hashnode asked whether an error text that names the next step would help, and whether I had varied the wording. So I ran a third test with this message instead:

```
lookup_order returned an empty result. Call lookup_order again with the same order_id.
```

## The set-up

- One model in both arms: qwen3.5 4B, temperature 0.7, the same prompt and tools.
- Both arms already had "Retry an empty lookup once." in the system prompt. The only difference is that one tool message.
- The 8 stock-note tasks, each with an empty result injected into the order lookup. I chose these tasks and this fault from run 2's failures.
- Pre-registered: the rule and the message were published before the first trial.
- No prediction this time. The first post had one before each run.

The test has three verdicts. PASS means the candidate (the arm under test) is not worse than the baseline (the reference) by more than 10 percentage points. BLOCK means it is worse by more than that. INCONCLUSIVE means it ran out of rounds. There is no verdict for "better". So the arm with the message took the baseline seat and run 2's set-up the candidate seat. Here, BLOCK favours the message.

## The result

BLOCK at round 2, the earliest possible round.

- With the message: 15 of 16 passed.
- With `null`: 2 of 16 passed.
- In 13 of the 16 pairs only the arm with the message passed. In 2 both passed, in 1 both failed, and in none did only the `null` arm pass.

On these 8 tasks, with this 4B model, this prompt and this one wording, the test decided that the arm with the message passes more often by more than 10 percentage points, under the test's stated assumptions. That is a threshold decision, not a measured size. The run stopped early, so 15 and 2 are counts, not rates.

## What it does not show

- That naming the next step is what helped. I tested one wording against `null`, and no message without a next step.
- Anything about the 12B model. It was in neither arm.
- Anything about the other 16 tasks, the other fault conditions or the full suite.

I did not run the retry in code: it hands the model the order, so the outcome is nearly fixed. A scripted test with no model, in the repository, shows how such a retry behaves.

## Two mistakes in my registration

A smoke run before the registration is not counted.

1. The registration says nothing was changed after the smoke run. The start script was changed: it gained its start checks.
2. It says 32 of the 4B's 34 failures under the empty result in run 2 were on these tasks. The store gives 33 of 34.

Both are published; neither changes the grid, the rule or the verdict.

The harness is my own open-source tool, ARCI.

- [Run 3 write-up](https://github.com/ajaysurya1221/agent-reliability-ci/blob/main/docs/results/order-desk-study.md#run-3-2026-11-16-a-message-at-the-empty-lookup-one-model-in-both-arms)

drafts.title: The verdict was BLOCK, and that was the good outcome
drafts.subtitle: Two readers asked for a further test of my 4B agent. My test cannot say "better", so I swapped the roles.
drafts.body_markdown:
My last post tested a small local model, qwen3.5 4B, on order-desk tasks with tools. Two readers asked for more. "Agentic Affairs" on dev.to asked for a retry of the empty lookup in code. "Halfcycle" on Hashnode asked whether an error text that names the next step would help, and whether I had varied the wording. I tested the second idea.

## The test cannot say "better"

My test compares two set-ups on the same tasks: a baseline (the current one) and a candidate (the proposed one). It has three verdicts. PASS: the candidate is not worse by more than 10 percentage points. BLOCK: it is worse by more than that. INCONCLUSIVE: it ran out of rounds.

None of these says "better". So I swapped the roles. The set-up with the new message took the baseline seat, the old set-up the candidate seat. BLOCK then means the old set-up does worse. Here, BLOCK was the good outcome for the message.

## The set-up

The same 4B model in both arms, on 8 stock-note tasks with an injected fault: the order lookup comes back empty. I chose these tasks and this fault from the earlier run's failures.

- One arm gets the text `null` for the empty result, as before.
- The other gets: "lookup_order returned an empty result. Call lookup_order again with the same order_id."
- Both arms already had "Retry an empty lookup once." in the system prompt.

The rule and the message were pre-registered: written down and pushed in a public commit before the first trial. Unlike the earlier runs, I wrote no prediction first. A small smoke run came before the registration; its trials are not counted.

## The result

BLOCK at round 2. 15 of 16 passed with the message, 2 of 16 without. In 13 of the 16 pairs only the arm with the message passed. In 2 both passed, in 1 both failed, and in none did only the arm without the message pass.

Under the test's stated assumptions, this supports one claim: on these 8 tasks, with this model, this prompt and this one wording, the arm with the message passes more often by more than 10 percentage points. It is a threshold decision, not a measured size. The run stopped early, so 15 and 2 are counts, not rates.

## What it does not show

- Whether naming the next step is what helped. I compared one wording with `null`, with no control message.
- Anything about the 12B model. It was in neither arm.
- Anything about the other 16 tasks, the other conditions or the full suite.

I did not run the code-retry variant. A scripted test with no model in the repository shows how such a retry behaves.

## Two published mistakes in my registration

The registration says nothing was changed after the smoke run, but the start script gained its start checks after it. It says 32 of the 4B's 34 earlier failures under the empty result were on these tasks; the records give 33 of 34. Neither changes the grid, the rule or the verdict.

## Check it yourself

The harness is my own open-source tool, ARCI.

- [Run 3 write-up](https://github.com/ajaysurya1221/agent-reliability-ci/blob/main/docs/results/order-desk-study.md#run-3-2026-11-16-a-message-at-the-empty-lookup-one-model-in-both-arms)
- [The pre-registration commit](https://github.com/ajaysurya1221/agent-reliability-ci/commit/c217ae6)
- [The raw records of every trial](https://github.com/ajaysurya1221/agent-reliability-ci/tree/main/docs/results/order-desk-study)
- [The first post](https://realornoise.hashnode.dev/i-tested-whether-a-4b-model-could-replace-a-12b-one-in-a-tool-using-agent-my-first-test-was-wrong)
- [Repository](https://github.com/ajaysurya1221/agent-reliability-ci)

I have not tested a message that reports the empty lookup but names no next step. If you have tried one, did it do as well?

judges.recommended_title: Two readers asked for one more test, so I ran it

rule_breaks: None that are hard breaks. Borderline: "a 4B model in a small order-desk agent often stopped after an order lookup came back empty" is a summary of behaviour. It rests on the first post's 21 of 26 under one combination, so it is supported, but "often" is wider than that and could be cut to "stopped".
Jargon: "The store gives 33 of 34." A new reader does not know what "the store" is.
Jargon: "The start script was changed: it gained its start checks." This is opaque to an outsider.
"arm" is used from the set-up onward and never explained.
best_parts: The opening shows the literal `null` and then the literal replacement message in code blocks. Within about 60 words a newcomer knows exactly what was swapped for what. It is the clearest hook of the three.
All three verdicts are defined in plain words, with baseline = "the reference" and candidate = "the arm under test", before the swap is explained. The swap then reads as logical, not confusing.
"The only difference is that one tool message." This makes the comparison obvious.
"Anything about the 12B model. It was in neither arm." This gives the reason as well as the limit.
The retry-in-code rationale is short and grounded in the pre-registration: "it hands the model the order, so the outcome is nearly fixed".
The closing question is concrete and is about the untested control.
hard_to_follow: The result does not appear in the first 60 words. A busy reader learns what was tested but has to reach the second section to see 15 of 16 against 2 of 16.
"A smoke run before the registration is not counted." This sits awkwardly as the lead line of the mistakes section, and "smoke run" is not explained.
"the grid" in "neither changes the grid, the rule or the verdict" is jargon. "the rule" means the decision rule, which is never said.

rule_breaks: Loose wording: "BLOCK then means the old set-up does worse." It drops "by more than 10 percentage points", so the bare sentence reads as a plain "worse" verdict. It should keep the threshold.

Title "The verdict was BLOCK, and that was the good outcome" is not a hard break, but "good outcome" leans evaluative and is mildly clickbait. It also makes BLOCK, the confusing part, the first thing a stranger meets.
Jargon: "the start script gained its start checks" is opaque to an outsider. "the grid" and "the rule" are not explained.
best_parts: It gives the clearest explanation of the swapped roles: "a baseline (the current one) and a candidate (the proposed one)", then a section titled "The test cannot say 'better'".
"I tested the second idea." This says plainly which reader request was taken up.
"the records give 33 of 34" is plainer than "the store".
The last line, "I have not tested a message that reports the empty lookup but names no next step. If you have tried one, did it do as well?", is honest about what was not tested.
The result is given as one compact paragraph.
hard_to_follow: The swap is explained before the reader knows what the "new message" is, so "the set-up with the new message" lands before the message has been shown.
The first 60 words give neither what was swapped nor the result.
"with no control message" is mild jargon for a casual reader.
"a further test" in the subtitle and "asked for more" are vague. A reader must go deep to learn the actual variable.

rule_breaks: Unclear limit: "An effect from setting these counts against run 2's: other seeds, another release." The rule is respected, but the sentence is cryptic. "other seeds, another release" means nothing to a new reader.
"baseline" and "candidate" are named but not explained in words: "The test compares two arms, a baseline and a candidate." The brief asks for a few-word explanation of each.
Only BLOCK is defined. PASS and INCONCLUSIVE are never mentioned, so the claim "It has no verdict for 'better'" has less to stand on.
Jargon: "The store gives 33 of 34." and "The start script gained its start checks after it."
best_parts: It quotes Halfcycle's actual question, "Did you try varying the error wording?", which is verified in hashnode-reply-1.md. "I had not." is a good, honest beat in the first post's voice.
The retry-in-code rationale is the most concrete of the three: "If the code repeats the lookup, the model gets the order without doing anything, so the result would say little about the model."
"the earliest round at which this rule can give that verdict" is more precise than "earliest possible round".
It says explicitly that the bound "holds under the test's stated assumptions, which the tool does not check".
hard_to_follow: The first 60 words are only about who asked what. Neither what was swapped nor the result appears until well past that point.
"I ran the nearest variant I could defend, the message." This mentions "the message" before any message has been introduced.
Its section on what the run does not show is the densest of the three, and its last bullet will lose a casual reader.
The ending, "If you have tried it: does a message that names no next step do as well?", has an unclear "it".

grafts: Into the winner's opening, add one plain result line within the first 60 words. For example, after the two code blocks: "With the message, 15 of 16 trials passed; with null, 2 of 16. Here is what that does and does not show." Keep it as counts, with no percentage.
From what-block-means, reuse the role glosses "a baseline (the current one) and a candidate (the proposed one)". They read better than "the reference" and "the arm under test".
From what-block-means, adapt "BLOCK then means the old set-up does worse", but add "by more than 10 percentage points" so it stays a threshold statement.
From readers-asked, add Halfcycle's verified quote "Did you try varying the error wording?" and the short "I had not." beat. It is the first post's voice of owning things.
From readers-asked, borrow "the model gets the order without doing anything" as a plainer version of "the outcome is nearly fixed".
From readers-asked, use "the earliest round at which this rule can give that verdict" instead of "the earliest possible round".
From what-block-means, say "the records give 33 of 34" instead of "the store gives".

From what-block-means, use the ending "I have not tested a message that reports the empty lookup but names no next step. If you have tried one, did it do as well?" It is clearer than the winner's question, and the winner's question is also fine.
missing_from_all: None of the drafts states the result (15 of 16 against 2 of 16, BLOCK favouring the message) within the first 60 words. A busy reader may leave before reaching it.
"arm" is never explained in any draft. Use "side" or "set-up", or gloss it once as "each of the two set-ups being compared".
"the rule" (meaning the registered decision rule) and "the grid" are not explained in any draft.
"the start script gained its start checks" is opaque in all three drafts. A plainer phrasing, if it matches the files, would be "I added checks to the script that starts the run".
None of the drafts says in a few words what "passed" means for a task, for example the agent completing the stock-note task correctly. A newcomer has to guess.
"smoke run" is not explained in any draft. Something like "a small trial run to check the set-up" would do.
